title: Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state
clue: An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response
conditions: Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons
access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
result: A reproducible application identity and baseline request
mechanics: TLS SNI, Host, redirects and cookies can select different applications. A response from the IP URL does not describe every hostname served by that listener.
checks:
```bash
curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/
curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/
```
example: Observation: the IP URL redirects to a hostname. Test: send the correct Host/SNI while routing to the assigned address. Illustrative output: a distinct application login appears. Interpretation: map that application separately.
verify: Record final URL, host, status, redirects, cookies and authentication context before comparing payload results.
failure: A redirect loop or generic default page may indicate a wrong host or missing session rather than a nonexistent application.

recognition.where: Request the assigned HTTP endpoint without following redirects blindly; inspect location, cookies and alternate scheme/hostname behavior.
recognition.commands:
```bash
curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/
curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/
```
recognition.sample:
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://HOSTNAME/
Set-Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE
recognition.spot: The hostname/scheme redirect identifies the application request context to reproduce.
recognition.confirm: Confirm the hostname routes to the assigned address and preserve its TLS/Host/session state.
recognition.enabled: The correct named request reaches a distinct application: map its functions.
recognition.ruledout: The candidate name produces only the default missing-host response: discard that virtual-host inference.
recognition.unknown: Redirect loops can mean missing cookies/host routing; repair the normal request before testing vulnerabilities.

procedure:
```bash curl -skL -D headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} bytes=%{size_download} type=%{content_type} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Decisive output:** record the scheme, hostname/`Host` header, port, redirects, page title, certificate names, server/framework clues and whether the view is anonymous or authenticated.
Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate ```bash curl -sk -H 'Host: CANDIDATE.DOMAIN' http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` Compare it with a random hostname. A different status alone is weak evidence; compare body, length, title and redirects.
Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects ```bash curl -skL -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Use a separate cookie jar per identity. Do not mix anonymous, ordinary-user and administrator evidence.
Variant — replay through Burp Community ```bash curl -sk -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Confirm the proxy listener is active on `127.0.0.1:8080`. Use `-k` only for the controlled lab because it disables destination-certificate verification.

next.when: DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response
next.requires: A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing

next.when: Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces
next.requires: A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons

next.when: JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata
next.requires: Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope

title: Map functions, roles and normal requests manually
clue: Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces
conditions: A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons
access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
result: An input/function/role map with concrete attack hypotheses
mechanics: The same functionality can expose different trust boundaries through object IDs, methods and roles. Changing one property while preserving request state makes differences interpretable.
example: Observation: a report download accepts a numeric ID. Test: compare objects owned by two authorized study accounts. Illustrative output: a lower role receives another account's report. Interpretation: proceed to an object-authorization method.
verify: Retain method, route, input location, identity and expected normal behavior; do not infer vulnerability from an interesting parameter name.
failure: Expired sessions, CSRF failures and malformed requests can imitate access-control differences; reproduce a valid baseline first.

recognition.where: Browse the site's normal account, export, upload and download features while recording requests in the browser/proxy.
recognition.sample:
Observed browser request:
GET /download?file=report.pdf
Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE
recognition.spot: The normal request exposes a file-selecting input discovered through functionality, not guessed from a payload list.
recognition.confirm: Find the actual input semantics, account/role and normal response before file/read/authorization tests.
recognition.enabled: Controlled comparisons prove a useful primitive: choose its method and remaining checks.
recognition.ruledout: The parameter only selects an allowlisted public report: discard unrestricted-path inference.
recognition.unknown: Unknown ownership or an expired session prevents interpreting differences; re-establish the baseline.

procedure:
For every visible function, capture one unchanged request in Burp Proxy history, send it to Repeater and record:

```text
METHOD PATH | CONTENT-TYPE | ACCESS CONTEXT/ROLE
INPUT LOCATION + NAME | BASELINE VALUE
STATUS | LENGTH/HASH | REDIRECT | MARKER/ERROR/TIME
OBJECT/FUNCTION SELECTED | NEXT ONE-VARIABLE TEST
```

Check login/registration/reset, profiles/objects, search/filter/pagination, download/export/preview, upload/import, administration and every JavaScript API call.

> **Next:** a browser-side restriction is not server authorization. Replay the raw request and change one field, object reference, method or access-context element at a time.

next.when: A request selects an object by ID/path and two authorized ownership contexts are available
next.requires: The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access

next.when: A download/path parameter or URL segment influences a local filename
next.requires: Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file

next.when: An upload/import/attachment function
next.requires: A valid upload request and permitted account; the server accepts and stores controlled bytes

next.when: An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints
next.requires: Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist

title: Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts
clue: JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata
conditions: Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope
access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
result: Hidden functionality, version clues or typed credential artifacts
mechanics: Client code and repository history can preserve endpoints and removed secrets. An exposed Git HEAD proves metadata exposure; repository completeness and secret validity require separate checks.
example: Observation: Git metadata is exposed. Test: recover only available objects and inspect history. Illustrative output: a removed database connection string. Interpretation: classify the account and validate current database access.
verify: Confirm actual file/history content and distinguish a historical secret from a usable current credential.
failure: A 200 soft-404 or incomplete object database is not a recovered repository. Compare known-missing paths and record missing history.

recognition.where: Inspect linked JavaScript/source, robots/sitemaps, relevant backups and a bounded Git metadata check from the mapped web application.
recognition.spot: The path and Git reference are investigation leads; neither proves a working secret or complete repository.
recognition.confirm: Compare missing-path controls, retrieve actual permitted artifacts and verify recovered history/account context.
recognition.enabled: Relevant source/history is recoverable and exposes a typed artifact: inspect it through the credential workflow.
recognition.ruledout: The same body is returned for arbitrary missing paths: reject the apparent metadata exposure.
recognition.unknown: HEAD without objects leaves repository recovery incomplete; document available content instead of inventing history.

procedure:
```bash
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/sitemap.xml
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/openapi.json
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/swagger.json
```

Also inspect HTML comments, hidden inputs, form actions, linked JavaScript, route strings, source-map references, cookies and response headers.

> **Decisive output:** a path, parameter, API schema, object identifier, component or secret-bearing artifact that creates a specific next request. Source disclosure is not command execution.

```bash
curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD
curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/config
```

> A readable `HEAD`/`config` supports exposed repository metadata. A `403`, redirect or generic template is not proof. Preserve the correct host header/base path.

If authorized, recover into a new local directory with a purpose-built tool and inspect locally:

```bash
git-dumper http://TARGET:PORT/.git/ repo-output
git -C repo-output status
git -C repo-output log --oneline --all --decorate
git -C repo-output log -p --all
```

`git-dumper` is an optional third-party helper; install on demand in an isolated environment only when the exposure has been confirmed. Manual object recovery is possible but slower.

```bash
rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|private[_-]?key' repo-output
git -C repo-output log --all -S'password' --oneline
git -C repo-output log --all -G'pass(word)?|secret|token' --oneline
```

Inspect candidate commits without dumping all history:

```bash
git -C repo-output show COMMIT -- PATH
git -C repo-output diff COMMIT^ COMMIT -- PATH
```

Validate freshness, identity and compatible use. Removed historical values are often rotated or environment-specific.

next.when: A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket
next.requires: Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol

next.when: A product/version clue, advisory or component-specific public PoC
next.requires: Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect

next.when: An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods
next.requires: A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type

title: Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering
clue: An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints
conditions: Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist
access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
mechanics: Discovery enumerates names; wildcard responses, redirects and soft-404 pages can make every guess appear valid. Confirm candidates through independent retrieval and behavior.
example: Observation: every path returns 200. Test: compare the missing-path body/length before filtering. Illustrative output: one candidate has a distinct export response. Interpretation: inspect that function manually.
verify: Open candidates and record their actual behavior; status/length alone is only a selection clue.
failure: Aggressive filters can hide genuine routes and rate limiting can fabricate differences; validate the baseline and reduce the request rate.

recognition.where: Establish the application's missing-path response, then run a bounded content search with the existing session/host context.
recognition.sample:
Missing control: status=200, body=DEFAULT_ERROR
Candidate /EXPORT_PATH/: status=200, body=EXPORT_FORM
recognition.spot: The candidate's actual function differs from the soft-404 control despite equal status codes.
recognition.confirm: Open it manually and identify authentication, roles, parameters and intended behavior.
recognition.enabled: Independent retrieval confirms an actual function: add its request to the behavior map.
recognition.ruledout: The candidate matches the wildcard error body: remove it from the useful queue.
recognition.unknown: Rate limiting or session expiry distorts response size; restore stable controls before filtering.

procedure:
Request a random nonexistent path first and record its status, length and body marker. ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt ``` > **Decisive output:** manually verified routes including useful `200`, redirect, `401`, `403` and `405` responses.
Variant — technology-aware extensions ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -x php,txt,bak,old,zip -t 10 -o gobuster-ext.txt ``` Choose extensions from observed stack evidence; do not spray every extension.
Variant — authenticated discovery ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -c 'SESSION=VALUE' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -t 10 -o gobuster-auth.txt ``` Use only the cookie or header that applies. An expired session can turn every result into the same login redirect.
Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST --exclude-length NOISE_LENGTH -t 10 -o gobuster-filtered.txt ``` Filtering without first confirming the noise response can hide a real path.

title: Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications
clue: DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response
conditions: A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing
access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
result: Additional verified applications on the same address
mechanics: Virtual-host routing uses the requested hostname. DNS resolution, HTTP Host and TLS SNI must be aligned when the server selects behavior at more than one layer.
example: Observation: a certificate suggests an internal application name. Test: resolve it to the assigned address while preserving SNI. Illustrative output: a separate administration interface. Interpretation: give it its own request and credential map.
verify: Compare candidate and nonexistent-host responses, including content and redirects; resolve to the intended scoped address.
failure: A default response for every host or an SNI mismatch makes the result inconclusive; do not treat every guessed hostname as a real application.

recognition.where: Collect hostnames from redirects, certificates, DNS and source; compare named requests against an invalid-host control.
recognition.sample:
Host HOSTNAME: application login page
Host INVALID_HOST: default server page
recognition.spot: A reproducible hostname-selected application is a new mapping target on the same address.
recognition.confirm: Keep Host/SNI/address consistent and confirm it is within assigned scope.
recognition.enabled: The named application has distinct verified behavior: give it its own session/function map.
recognition.ruledout: All candidate hosts receive the same default body: discard the claimed distinct application.
recognition.unknown: TLS routing or local DNS is wrong: fix that context before deciding a vhost is absent.

procedure:
```bash
gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt
```

Alternative with automatic calibration:

```bash
ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.DOMAIN' -ac -o ffuf-vhosts.json
```

> **Failure cue:** uniform status/length may be the default vhost. Compare each candidate with a random host header before adding it to the application map.

title: Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties
clue: An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods
conditions: A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type
access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
result: A parameter/object/method inventory and testable authorization or injection hypothesis
mechanics: APIs enforce security at route, object and property boundaries. A valid JSON body can be accepted while a sensitive field is ignored; test its persisted effect separately.
example: Observation: an API response includes a role property. Test: compare documented writable fields and a controlled update. Illustrative output: the field is ignored and privilege is unchanged. Interpretation: that mass-assignment hypothesis is disproven; investigate other boundaries.
verify: Prove which input is consumed and whether state changes persist in an independent read.
failure: HTTP 400/415 may indicate encoding/schema rather than security enforcement. Keep a valid request before changing permissions-related properties.

recognition.where: Capture a valid API request, inspect its schema/client code and compare allowed methods and controlled object/role contexts.
recognition.spot: The actual object, method and writable input are known; returned owner/role fields are only candidate security boundaries.
recognition.confirm: Determine field binding, ownership, persistence and server authorization with controlled accounts.
recognition.enabled: A protected field/action changes under a lower role and is independently verified: select its authorization method.
recognition.ruledout: The server ignores the sensitive field and privileges remain unchanged: reject that assignment hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Malformed JSON or wrong content type makes a failed request inconclusive; reproduce the valid update first.

procedure:
GET parameter names:

```bash
ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/PATH?FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-get.json
```

POST form parameter names:

```bash
ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/PATH -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -d 'known=value&FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-post.json
```

Object values with an authenticated API:

```bash
ffuf -w NUMBERS -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/FUZZ' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -mc all -fc 404 -o object-values.json
```

> **Decisive output:** a manually reproduced parameter or value that changes application behavior. Tool outliers are candidates, not confirmed access-control flaws.

```bash
curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH
curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH
curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/login
```

> **Interpretation:** `405` can establish that a route exists but rejects the method. Validation errors can reveal required fields. A token establishes only the authorization demonstrated by a later request.

```text
PATH | METHOD | IDENTITY/ROLE | OBJECT/PROPERTY | RESULT | NEXT
```

next.when: API objects expose role, ownership or security-sensitive properties
next.requires: The server binds an untrusted property to a persistent security-relevant field without checking permission

next.when: A request selects an object by ID/path and two authorized ownership contexts are available
next.requires: The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access

next.when: An input appears in a command-like operation or causes shell-dependent behavior
next.requires: Input reaches command execution with an exploitable parsing boundary; process identity/runtime can perform the selected proof

next.when: Database errors or controlled true/false response differences
next.requires: Input reaches a SQL query; a valid request and stable response baseline exist

next.when: Untrusted input reaches an executable HTML/JavaScript context
next.requires: Payload reaches a browser execution sink; any useful privileged action additionally needs a victim context, same-origin access and a valid request state

next.when: URL import, preview, webhook or fetch behavior
next.requires: The application server performs a controllable request; destination/protocol policy and its network position permit the selected resource
